facts.text: Watch Cheryl's piano book on the subway: as she steps onto the platform, it flips between upside down and right-side up from shot to shot.
The creepy man in the metal mask is Michele Soavi, Lamberto Bava's assistant director. He also directed the movie-within-the-movie, and later made The Church and Cemetery Man.
The US release has a mono mix with extra sound effects, like a demon growl and slicing sound over the title. Every other release print has the original Dolby Stereo mix.
Demons began as one story in a planned three-part horror anthology by writer Dardano Sacchetti, modeled on Mario Bava's Black Sabbath. Director Lamberto Bava liked this segment best and expanded it.
Natasha Hovey (Cheryl) was born in Beirut to an American musician father and a Dutch mother. She debuted at 16 in Carlo Verdone's Acqua e sapone and later retired in Paris.
Producer Dario Argento was fresh from Phenomena (1985) and wanted to produce more films, as he had with Dawn of the Dead. Demons became his producing project with Lamberto Bava.
Director Lamberto Bava, son of horror master Mario Bava, has called Demons his personal favorite of all the films he has directed.
The Metropol exterior was a real Berlin club at the time. Its name and logo, even on the invitation, weren't made for the film. The building still stands and hosts horror conventions.
Nicoletta Elmi, the little girl from Dario Argento's Deep Red, made Demons her final film.
A poster in the lobby is for Argento's 1972 Four Flies on Grey Velvet, a nod to the producer. Other lobby posters include No Nukes, Metropolis and AC/DC.
A blind man going to the movies was an intentional ironic joke by the filmmakers.
Demons was shot in about nine weeks in June and July 1985, on location in West Berlin and at De Paolis Studios in Rome.
Fiore Argento, who plays Hannah, is the daughter of producer and co-writer Dario Argento and the older half-sister of Asia Argento.
Co-writer Franco Ferrini says his contribution was postponing the arrival of the demons, which originally showed up much earlier in the script.
Producer Fabrizio De Angelis, shown the early treatment, wanted to save money by using footage from Lucio Fulci's films as the movie-within-the-movie. Bava and Sacchetti went elsewhere.
The film-within-the-film digs up Nostradamus' tomb. A myth says his corpse wore a medallion with the date of its own disinterment, and the grave robbers were supposedly cursed and shot.
Demons was made on a budget of about $1.8 million.
The tagline: 'They will make cemeteries their cathedrals and the cities will be your tombs.'
Makeup effects artist Sergio Stivaletti handled the demon transformations. He became Dario Argento's regular effects collaborator, and Michele Soavi later hired him for The Church and Cemetery Man.
Story writer Dardano Sacchetti had earlier written for Lucio Fulci's Gates of Hell trilogy and Mario Bava's A Bay of Blood.
Demons is referenced in Scream 2 (1997), 28 Days Later (2002), Silent Hill (1999) and The Exorcist: Believer (2023).
Writer-director Luigi Cozzi says in a Blu-ray featurette that Demons was 'spawned out of cost overruns' on Dario Argento's Phenomena (1985).
Richard Scheib of Moria called Demons 'absurdly entertaining' and described it as a blend of The Evil Dead and The Purple Rose of Cairo.
Composer Claudio Simonetti, keyboardist of the band Goblin, says the Demons score was built on a drum machine. He played most of the parts on keyboards.
The name of the cinema, Metropol, shows up as a building in the first Silent Hill video game.
Director Lamberto Bava keeps the camera moving to hide makeup seams, unlike Lucio Fulci, who held shots on his gore effects long enough to show how they worked.
Demons grossed about 1.2 billion lire in Italy, the 39th biggest film of 1985, ahead of Cat's Eye, Silver Bullet and A Nightmare on Elm Street.
The Italian cut used 'Dynamite' by Scorpions on the soundtrack. The US version swapped it for Pretty Maids' 'Night Danger.' Mötley Crüe, Billy Idol and Accept songs are also featured.
Director Lamberto Bava says making Demons reunited producer Dario Argento with screenwriter Dardano Sacchetti, who had fallen out before.
The cocaine scene in the car caused controversy and was censored in nearly every country.
Kim Newman wrote in Monthly Film Bulletin that Demons suffered from the same over-emphatic tone as Dario Argento's own Phenomena.
The UK BBFC cut 1 minute 5 seconds, including eye gougings, a demon vomiting on a woman, and cocaine being scraped off a woman's breast with a razor blade.
Ottaviano Dell'Acqua, the worm-faced ghoul in Lucio Fulci's Zombie, did stunt work on Demons and later recalled it in a Blu-ray featurette.
Demons gets name-checked in Brain Damage, Remote Control and The Toxic Avenger Part III.
Geretta Geretta says Italian casting goes by pictures first. She joked she schemed to keep Rosemary alive for Demons 2, but was out of town when it was made.
Lamberto Bava started as assistant director to his father Mario, then directed his first solo feature, Macabre, in 1980.
Germany cut 41 seconds for an FSK-18 rating, then indexed and banned the film anyway. The ban was lifted only in August 2023, though it was filmed in Berlin.
Author Alan Jones claims on the Blu-ray that director Lamberto Bava's loud, 'shouty' style drove Fiore Argento, Dario Argento's daughter, to quit acting.
The glowing demon eyes were improvised on set: actors wore refractive paper as they approached the camera, which created the effect.
Bravo ranked Demons at number 53 on its 100 Scariest Movie Moments countdown.
Roy Bava, son of director Lamberto Bava, describes his father on the Demons set as 'a wild beast.'
Demons holds a 73% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 15 reviews.
Spot the AC/DC and No Nukes posters in the lobby. They're likely 1980 concert and documentary films.
In Germany, Demons was released as 'Dämonen 2', a sequel to the actual second film, which was released there as the first.
As the helicopter first crashes into the cinema, the casing around the rotor base is broken in one shot and intact in the next.
Urbano Barberini (George) starred in Dario Argento's Opera, where his voice was replaced with a deeper one in the English dub.
Kim Newman wrote in Sight & Sound that Demons and its sequel are guilty pleasures whose 'demented glee' makes them ideal party horror movies.
Demons reached North American grindhouses and drive-ins in May 1986, after opening in Europe in fall 1985.
Michele Soavi's The Church (1989) began as Demons 3. Bava's TV movie The Ogre was released abroad as Demons III, and his Black Sunday remake was retitled Demons 5.
Leonard Maltin gave Demons 1 1/2 out of 4 stars, criticizing its lack of characterization, logic and plot.
Stay put during the credits: there's a jump scare about halfway through as a character turns demonic.
